name: Mecca
tagline: The holiest city in Islam, for Hajj and Umrah
summary: The birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and the direction of prayer for Muslims everywhere. Millions come each year for Umrah, and for Hajj in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah. Only Muslims may enter the city; non-Muslim travellers can learn about it in Jeddah and Medina's museums.
seasonNote: Hajj dates move about 11 days earlier each year with the Islamic calendar; Ramadan, especially the last ten nights, is the busiest time for Umrah. Summer passes 45°C.
arrival: Only Muslims may enter Mecca; checkpoints on every road enforce this. Fly to Jeddah, then take the Haramain high-speed train (about 35 minutes) or a bus. Umrah is booked through the official Nusuk app; Hajj needs a Hajj visa through an authorised operator or your country's quota.
gettingAround: Most hotels are walking distance from the Grand Mosque; buses and the Mashaer metro (during Hajj) serve the holy sites at Mina, Muzdalifah and Arafat.
cashTip: Cards are widely accepted; carry riyals for small shops and taxis.
foodTip: Eat simply between prayers: Al Baik fried chicken, mandi rice with lamb, and Zamzam water, which is free throughout the mosque.
buyTip: Prayer mats, misbaha prayer beads, perfume oils, dates and Zamzam water in sealed containers for home.
baseArea: The hotels around the Grand Mosque, especially the Abraj Al-Bait towers and Ibrahim Al Khalil Road

connections.note: Flights land in Jeddah, then the train to Mecca.

items.name: Masjid al-Haram and the Kaaba
items.summary: The Great Mosque surrounding the Kaaba, the centre of Muslim worship, where pilgrims perform tawaf and sa'i.
items.expect: Muslims only; huge crowds at prayer times and in Ramadan; ihram clothing is required for Umrah.
items.tip: Perform tawaf late at night or after Fajr for the calmest time; the upper floors are less crowded.
items.why: The holiest site in Islam.
flow: Enter through King Abdulaziz Gate or King Fahd Gate.
Tawaf around the Kaaba, then sa'i between Safa and Marwah.

items.name: Clock Tower Museum
items.summary: A museum of astronomy and timekeeping near the top of the clock tower, with a viewing deck over the Grand Mosque.
items.expect: Timed tickets; queues at peak season.
items.tip: Go at sunset for the view of the mosque lighting up.
items.why: The only place to see the whole Grand Mosque from above.
flow: Lifts from the Abraj Al-Bait mall.

items.name: Jabal al-Nour and the Cave of Hira
items.summary: The mountain cave where the Prophet received the first revelation of the Quran.
items.expect: A steep climb of about 1,200 steps, an hour or more; very hot by day.
items.tip: Start before dawn with water and a torch; the Hira Cultural District at the foot explains the story.
items.why: A place of deep meaning and a sweeping view of the city.
flow: Taxi to the foot of the mountain.
Climb to the cave, then the cultural centre below.

items.name: Mount Arafat
items.summary: The hill where pilgrims stand in prayer on the Day of Arafah, the peak of Hajj, and where the Prophet gave his Farewell Sermon.
items.expect: Quiet outside Hajj; extremely crowded on the day itself.
items.tip: Many Umrah pilgrims visit Mina, Muzdalifah and Arafat on a guided ziyarah tour.
items.why: The heart of the Hajj.
flow: Ziyarah tour or taxi, 20 km east.
Jabal al-Rahmah, then Muzdalifah and Mina on the way back.

items.name: Mina
items.summary: The valley of white tents where pilgrims stay during Hajj and perform the stoning of the Jamarat.
items.expect: Nearly empty outside Hajj.
items.tip: See it as part of a ziyarah tour to understand the Hajj route.
items.why: Where millions camp for the Hajj days.
flow: Jamarat Bridge, then the tent city.

items.name: Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques Architecture
items.wiki: Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques Architecture
items.summary: A museum of the history of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque, with old Kaaba doors and the kiswah.
items.expect: Small and calm.
items.tip: Pair it with the Kiswa factory nearby, where the Kaaba's black cloth is woven.
items.why: The story of the mosques' buildings through the centuries.

items.name: Al Baik
items.summary: Saudi Arabia's beloved fried chicken chain, with branches beside the Grand Mosque.
items.expect: Queues at every prayer break.
items.tip: Order the broasted chicken meal with garlic sauce.
items.why: A rite of passage for every pilgrim.
flow: Eat in your hotel or the plaza.

items.name: Abraj Al-Bait food court
items.summary: Several floors of restaurants and food stalls in the clock tower mall facing the mosque.
items.expect: Crowded after each prayer.
items.tip: Eat between prayer times to avoid the rush.
items.why: The easiest meal close to the mosque.
flow: Enter the mall from the plaza.
Pick from Arabic, Asian and Turkish counters.

items.name: Al Aziziyah mandi restaurants
items.summary: A district of family restaurants serving mandi and kabsa, rice slow-cooked with lamb or chicken.
items.expect: Floor seating in family rooms is common.
items.tip: Order one large platter to share.
items.why: The best value hearty meals in Mecca.
flow: Taxi 15 minutes east of the mosque.
Share a platter of lamb mandi.

name: Medina
summary: Islam's second holiest city, where the Prophet Muhammad lived his last years and is buried. Most pilgrims combine it with Umrah in Mecca. The Prophet's Mosque and the area around it are for Muslims only, but non-Muslim visitors may now visit the rest of the city, its museums and Mount Uhud.
seasonNote: Busiest in Ramadan and the weeks around Hajj; summer days pass 45°C.
arrival: Prince Mohammad bin Abdulaziz Airport is 20 minutes from the centre; the Haramain high-speed train links Mecca (about 2 hours 15 minutes) and Jeddah.
gettingAround: Hotels surround the Prophet's Mosque; taxis and ziyarah tour buses reach Quba, Uhud and the museums.
cashTip: Cards widely accepted; riyals for date shops and taxis.
foodTip: Medina is famous for its dates, especially Ajwa; try them with Arabic coffee.
buyTip: Ajwa and Sukkari dates from the dates market, perfume oils and prayer beads.
baseArea: The hotels around the Prophet's Mosque (Muslims), or Quba and Al Aziziyah for non-Muslim visitors

items.name: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi
items.summary: The Prophet's Mosque, with the Green Dome over his tomb and the Rawdah, a space Muslims consider a garden of paradise.
items.expect: Muslims only; a visit to the Rawdah must be booked in the Nusuk app; giant umbrellas shade the courtyards.
items.tip: Book your Rawdah slot as soon as you arrive; late-night slots are easiest to get.
items.why: The second holiest site in Islam.
flow: Rawdah at your slot, then greetings at the Prophet's tomb.
items.book: Rawdah slot in the Nusuk app

items.name: Quba Mosque
items.summary: The first mosque in Islam, built by the Prophet on his arrival from Mecca.
items.expect: Open to Muslims for prayer; busiest on Saturday mornings, following the Prophet's practice.
items.tip: Walk the new Quba Walkway from the Prophet's Mosque, about 3 km.
items.why: A prayer here is said to carry the reward of an Umrah.
flow: Pray two rak'ahs, then the date shops outside.

items.name: Mount Uhud and the Martyrs' Cemetery
items.summary: The mountain where the Battle of Uhud took place in 625, with the graves of the martyrs including Hamza.
items.expect: Open to all; modest dress required.
items.tip: Climb the small Archers' Hill opposite for the view.
items.why: One of the key places in early Islamic history.

items.name: Dar Al Madinah Museum
items.summary: A museum of the history and architecture of Medina, with detailed models of the city in the Prophet's time.
items.expect: Open to all; guided tours in several languages.
items.tip: A good first stop for non-Muslim visitors.
items.why: The clearest introduction to the city.
flow: Models of old Medina, then the architecture halls.

items.name: Hejaz Railway Station Museum
items.summary: The Ottoman-era terminus of the railway from Damascus, with old locomotives and a museum.
items.expect: Open to all; small.
items.tip: Pair with the nearby Anbariya Mosque.
items.why: The story of the railway built to bring pilgrims from Istanbul.
flow: Station hall, then the engines outside.

items.name: Seven Mosques
items.summary: Small mosques at the site of the Battle of the Trench, including the Al-Fath mosque.
items.expect: Part of most ziyarah tours.
items.tip: Combine with the Qiblatain Mosque, where the direction of prayer changed to Mecca.
items.why: Key places from the Prophet's life in Medina.

items.name: Medina dates market
items.summary: Rows of shops selling dozens of kinds of dates, from Ajwa to Sukkari and Safawi, with free tastings.
items.expect: Prices vary a lot by grade.
items.tip: Taste before buying and ask for date-filled ma'amoul cookies.
items.why: Medina's dates are famous across the Muslim world.
flow: Near the Prophet's Mosque or by Quba.
Taste three or four kinds, then buy a box.

items.name: Al Baik
items.summary: The Saudi fried chicken chain, a favourite of pilgrims.
items.expect: Queues after each prayer.
items.tip: Go between prayer times.
items.why: Quick, cheap and loved.

items.name: Al Aziziyah and Quba Road restaurants
items.summary: Family restaurants along Quba Road serving Hejazi, Yemeni, Turkish and South Asian food.
items.expect: Busy after Isha prayer.
items.tip: Try saleeg, Hejazi creamy rice with chicken.
items.why: A wide choice away from the hotel crowds.

name: Riyadh
tagline: Desert capital, mud-brick Diriyah and the Edge of the World
summary: The fast-changing Saudi capital, with the restored mud-brick birthplace of the Saudi state at Diriyah, good museums and the cliffs of the Tuwaiq escarpment an hour away.
seasonNote: Summer passes 45°C; Riyadh Season brings concerts and festivals from October to March.
arrival: King Khalid International Airport is 35 km north; taxis and the Riyadh Metro line 4 link the city.
gettingAround: Use the Riyadh Metro, ride-hailing apps or a car; the city is spread out and not walkable.
foodTip: Najdi dishes: jareesh (cracked wheat), kabsa, margoog stew and qursan, with Saudi coffee and dates.
buyTip: Oud perfume, dates and Bedouin crafts in the souqs around Masmak.
baseArea: Olaya for hotels and restaurants, or near Diriyah

connections.note: Frequent flights; a train link is under construction.

items.name: At-Turaif, Diriyah
items.summary: The mud-brick palaces of the first Saudi capital, restored with museums and light shows.
items.expect: Ticketed evening visits; much of Diriyah is still under construction.
items.tip: Go at sunset, then eat at the Bujairi Terrace across the wadi.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and the birthplace of the Saudi state.

items.name: Masmak Fortress
items.summary: The clay fort whose capture in 1902 began the founding of modern Saudi Arabia.
items.expect: Free; closes for prayers.
items.tip: Walk on to Souq Al Zal for antiques and carpets.
items.why: The founding story of the country.
flow: Metro or taxi to Al Dirah.
Fort, Justice Square, then Souq Al Zal.

items.name: National Museum of Saudi Arabia
items.summary: A large museum of Arabian history from prehistory to the founding of the kingdom.
items.expect: Air-conditioned; allow two hours.
items.tip: Pair with the Murabba Palace in the same park.
items.why: The best overview of the Arabian Peninsula's past.
flow: Taxi to King Abdulaziz Historical Center.
Halls in order, then Murabba Palace.

items.name: Kingdom Centre Sky Bridge
items.summary: A glass bridge across the top of the city's landmark tower, 300 metres up.
items.expect: A two-lift ride; queues at sunset.
items.tip: Go at dusk to see the city lights come on.
items.why: The classic Riyadh skyline view.

items.name: Edge of the World
items.summary: Sheer 300-metre cliffs of the Tuwaiq escarpment with a view over an ancient caravan plain.
items.expect: About 90 minutes each way, the last part on rough desert track; 4x4 or tour only. Closed in hot months.
items.tip: Go with a tour for sunset and a picnic dinner.
items.why: The most dramatic landscape near Riyadh.
flow: Walk the cliff edge, stay for sunset.

items.name: Boulevard City
items.summary: An entertainment district of shows, fountains, restaurants and rides, at its busiest in Riyadh Season.
items.expect: Ticketed; crowded on weekend nights (Thursday and Friday).
items.tip: Check the Riyadh Season calendar for concerts.
items.why: A look at how fast Saudi social life is changing.

items.name: Najd Village
items.summary: A restaurant built like a traditional Najdi house, with floor seating and regional dishes.
items.expect: Large shared platters; family and singles sections.
items.tip: Order the Najdi sampler to try jareesh, margoog and qursan.
items.why: The classic place to try central Arabian food.
flow: Coffee and dates, then the platter.

items.name: Bujairi Terrace
items.summary: A dining terrace of about 20 restaurants overlooking the At-Turaif palaces.
items.expect: Pricey and smart; book at weekends.
items.tip: Sit facing At-Turaif when it is lit at night.
items.why: Riyadh's most beautiful setting for dinner.

items.name: Mama Noura
items.summary: A long-running Riyadh favourite for shawarma, juices and grills.
items.expect: Busy late into the night.
items.tip: Order the chicken shawarma and a fresh cocktail juice.
items.why: The city's best-known cheap meal.

name: Jeddah
tagline: Gateway to Mecca, coral-stone old town and the Red Sea
summary: The Red Sea port where most pilgrims arrive, with a coral-stone old town of carved wooden balconies, a long corniche and some of the best reef diving in the region.
seasonNote: Humid and hot from May to October; winter is warm and pleasant.
arrival: King Abdulaziz International Airport is 20 km north; the Haramain train runs to Mecca and Medina.
gettingAround: Ride-hailing apps and taxis; Al-Balad is walkable.
cashTip: Cards everywhere; small cash for the souq.
foodTip: Hejazi food: ful medames for breakfast, mutabbaq, sayadiyah fish rice and Al Baik, which started here.
buyTip: Perfume, spices and textiles in Al-Balad's souqs.
baseArea: The North Corniche or near Al-Balad

items.name: Al-Balad historic district
items.summary: The old town of coral-stone tower houses with carved wooden rawasheen balconies and busy souqs.
items.expect: Some houses are under restoration; it comes alive after dark.
items.tip: Visit Nassif House, then walk the souqs in the evening.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and the gateway pilgrims walked through for centuries.
flow: Nassif House, Souq Al Alawi, then dinner in the lanes.

items.name: Jeddah Corniche and King Fahd's Fountain
items.summary: A seafront promenade with the world's tallest fountain, shooting water over 300 metres.
items.expect: The fountain runs most evenings.
items.tip: Walk the waterfront park at sunset.
items.why: Where Jeddah comes out in the evening.
flow: Walk south to see the fountain.

items.name: Al-Rahma Mosque
items.summary: The 'floating mosque' built on stilts over the Red Sea.
items.expect: Non-Muslims can see it from outside; modest dress.
items.tip: Go at high tide or sunset for the reflection.
items.why: The most photographed mosque in Jeddah.

items.name: Red Sea diving at Obhur
items.summary: Coral reefs and wrecks off the northern beaches, with dive centres and beach clubs.
items.expect: Most beaches are private clubs with a day fee.
items.tip: Book a boat dive to the reefs off Abu Tair.
items.why: Some of the healthiest reefs in the Red Sea.
flow: Dive centre, boat to the reef.

items.name: Hayy Jameel
items.summary: An arts complex of galleries, studios and a cinema.
items.expect: Closed on some weekdays; free exhibitions.
items.tip: Check the programme for film screenings.
items.why: The centre of Jeddah's contemporary art scene.

items.name: Al-Balad street food
items.summary: Night stalls and small shops selling mutabbaq, balila chickpeas, kebda liver and sweets.
items.expect: Busiest from 9 pm.
items.tip: Try mutabbaq, a stuffed folded flatbread, hot off the griddle.
items.why: The food of old Jeddah.

items.name: Al Baik
items.summary: The fried chicken chain that started in Jeddah in 1974.
items.expect: Queues at peak times.
items.tip: Try the spicy chicken meal.
items.why: A Saudi institution in its home city.

items.name: Jeddah fish market restaurants
items.summary: Choose fish at the market and have it grilled or fried at a restaurant nearby.
items.expect: Early morning is the busiest market time.
items.tip: Order sayadiyah, fish with spiced brown rice.
items.why: Jeddah is a fishing port first.
flow: Have it cooked at a neighbouring restaurant.

name: AlUla
summary: A desert valley of sandstone outcrops holding Hegra, the Nabataean sister city of Petra, along with a mud-brick old town and the mirrored Maraya concert hall.
seasonNote: Winter days are warm and nights cold; summer is very hot and many tours pause.
arrival: AlUla airport has flights from Riyadh and Jeddah; it is about 4 hours by road from Medina.
gettingAround: Sites are spread out and visited on ticketed tours with shuttle buses; a car helps.
cashTip: Cards for tickets; little need for cash.
foodTip: Local dates and citrus from the oasis, and Saudi coffee in the old town.
buyTip: Dates, crafts and local honey in the old town.
baseArea: Near AlUla Old Town, or a desert resort

items.name: Hegra
items.summary: More than 100 Nabataean tombs carved into sandstone outcrops, including the lone Tomb of Lihyan son of Kuza.
items.expect: Visits are by timed guided tour with shuttle buses.
items.tip: Book the late-afternoon tour for the warm light on the tombs.
items.why: Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Qasr al-Farid, Jabal Ithlib, then the main tomb groups.

items.name: Elephant Rock
items.summary: A 50-metre sandstone outcrop shaped like an elephant, with a lounge in the sand beside it.
items.expect: Open evenings; busy at sunset.
items.tip: Arrive before sunset and stay as the rock is lit.
items.why: AlUla's most famous natural landmark.
flow: Walk around the rock, then sit by the fire pits.

items.name: AlUla Old Town
items.summary: A maze of hundreds of mud-brick houses below a hilltop castle, now restored with cafés and shops.
items.expect: Best in the evening when the lanes are lit.
items.tip: Climb to AlUla Castle for the view over the oasis.
items.why: The heart of the old caravan town.

items.name: Dadan and Jabal Ikmah
items.summary: The ruins of the Dadanite and Lihyanite kingdoms and a canyon of ancient inscriptions called an open-air library.
items.expect: Guided tours; little shade.
items.tip: Do Jabal Ikmah in the morning when the inscriptions are clearest.
items.why: Older than Hegra, and far less visited.
flow: Shuttle tour from the visitor centre.
Dadan tombs, then the Ikmah canyon.

items.name: Maraya
items.summary: A concert hall clad entirely in mirrors, reflecting the desert canyon around it.
items.expect: The inside is open for concerts and the restaurant.
items.tip: See it at sunset, when the mirrors glow.
items.why: The largest mirrored building in the world.
flow: Walk around the outside, then the rooftop restaurant.

items.name: Harrat Viewpoint
items.summary: A lookout on the volcanic plateau above the AlUla valley.
items.expect: A winding drive up; cold in winter evenings.
items.tip: Go for sunset with a jacket.
items.why: The widest view over the whole valley.

items.name: Maraya Social
items.summary: A rooftop restaurant on the mirrored Maraya building, with desert views.
items.expect: Expensive; book for sunset.
items.tip: Ask for a table facing the canyon.
items.why: The most dramatic dining room in AlUla.

items.name: Old Town cafés and restaurants
items.summary: Cafés and restaurants along the restored lanes of the Old Town and Al Jadidah arts district.
items.expect: Opens in the late afternoon.
items.tip: Try Saudi coffee with local dates.
items.why: The easiest dinner after a day at the sites.

items.name: AlUla farmers' market
items.summary: A weekend market of oasis produce, dates, citrus, honey and home cooking.
items.expect: Weekend mornings in the cool season only.
items.tip: Buy citrus and dates straight from the growers.
items.why: The taste of the oasis.
